Hi Rafael / team,

Thanks again for the demo earlier — useful discussion. I promised to follow up with the performance / SLO constraints so you can size a proof-of-concept and give rough cost/back-of-envelope GPU sizing. High level: our product is a customer-facing chat + some periodic batch generation jobs. Key details from our side: 

- Primary user flow: interactive chat (web + mobile) — needs token-level streaming (clients show responses as tokens arrive).
- Steady-state traffic: ~30 requests/sec during business hours (US), each request averages ~250 input tokens and ~180 output tokens.
- Peak bursts: up to ~120 requests/sec for 3–10 minute spikes (end-of-month reporting + marketing activations).
- Long-running generation: ~20% of requests are long (400–1,200 output tokens) — used for report generation.
- Latency targets: for interactive chat we want p95 initial-token latency <= 200ms ideally, and end-to-end p95 for short responses <= 400ms. For long-run jobs we tolerate higher p95 but prefer predictable throughput.
- Concurrency: target support for 500 concurrent chat sessions (many idle / streaming).

Attached a sample traffic file (sample-traffic.json) and a simple sheet with hourly QPS (throughput-sizing.xlsx).

Next steps: could you confirm the info above and let us know what assumptions you need (e.g., tokenization, model family, quantization tolerance) to propose an initial sizing? We're aiming for a 2-week PoC to validate perf.

Best,
Sofia Chen

Thanks Rafael — answers inline below.

1) For p95 initial-token <= 200ms we mean time-to-first-token (server-side + network) as experienced by the client. That is our hard interactive target for short responses.
2) Token-level streaming is preferred for chat UX. We can tolerate small batching on the server (e.g., 50–100 token chunks) if it materially improves throughput vs per-token overhead.
3) Max sequence length: typically inputs are short (<= 512 tokens) but in long reports we can see inputs up to 1,000 tokens. So plan for worst-case total sequence (input+output) of ~2,200 tokens for the long jobs.
4) Peak bursts are usually short: 3–10 minutes, driven by marketing events. They are mostly many short chats (spikes in QPS) — long requests are less concurrent.

One other ask: we have a strict cost target for PoC — can you provide an estimate for dedicated GPUs vs hosted burst under these workloads? We'll need a ballpark before the sizing call.

Hi Sofia — thanks for the clarifications and the updated traffic sample. Based on the patterns you described, here are our initial sizing assumptions and recommendations for the PoC (ballpark numbers; we will refine after ingesting sample-traffic.json):

Assumptions
- Mix: 70% short chats (<= 200 output tokens), 30% long jobs (400–1,200 output tokens).
- Steady-state: 30 req/s (short-heavy), Peak: 120 req/s for ~5 minutes (mostly short chats).
- Tokenization: conservative worst-case total sequence length up to 2,200 tokens for long requests.
- Streaming: token-level streaming preferred; we'll use chunked streaming (50 token chunks) as a pragmatic tradeoff.

Sizing guidance (initial)
- Model family: for interactive latency targets we recommend trying a quantized rw-7b or rw-13b variant (depends on quality bar).
- Throughput estimates (per GPU, runs depend on model and quantization):
  - rw-7b quantized (int8-ish): ~1,200–1,800 tokens/sec per GPU for generation workloads.
  - rw-13b quantized: ~700–1,100 tokens/sec per GPU.
- For short-chat steady-state (30 req/s * avg 180 tokens output ~5,400 tokens/sec): 3–5 rw-7b GPUs could cover sustained throughput with margin using batching (continuous batching + streaming chunks).
- For peaks (120 req/s * avg 180 tokens ~21,600 tokens/sec): would need ~12–18 rw-7b GPUs if you want to absorb peaks without queueing. Autoscaling/bursting can be used to handle short peaks more cost-effectively.
- Long jobs: these are throughput-bound. Recommend separate worker pool (batch queue) to avoid impacting interactive tail latencies. For 20% long-job traffic, add 2–4 dedicated GPUs tuned for long-seq generation (larger batch sizes).

Latency notes and levers
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT) depends on model cold-start, batching delay, and kernel perf. To hit p95 TTFT <= 200ms for short responses we recommend:
  - Keep a small warm pool of pre-warmed model workers to avoid cold start (1–2 reserved workers).
  - Limit batching delay to <= 20–30ms (continuous batching) and use chunked streaming to reduce per-token overhead.
  - Use lightweight quantized models; rw-7b int8-like variant has better TTFT than larger models.

Recommended PoC config
- Option A (cost-optimized hosted PoC): start with 4 rw-7b quantized workers with autoscaling to burst up to 12 for short peaks. Use dedicated cache for system prompts and prefix caching.
- Option B (dedicated PoC pool): 6 x A100-equivalent GPUs (quantized rw-7b) with a separate 2–GPU batch pool for long jobs.

Deliverables for the sizing call
- We'll produce a short spreadsheet (attached) with tokens/sec estimates, expected QPS coverage, and cost ballparks for hosted vs dedicated.
- Next: Rafael / I can run a quick calibration run using your sample-traffic.json and return refined tokens/sec and GPU counts.

Can we lock the 09:30 PST call? I’ll bring a short sizing spreadsheet and a proposed PoC plan.
